primaries.primaryEn: Abhinavagupta opens his great book with a prayer to the highest reality. In simple words: may that supreme home — the Trika truth which is pure oneness, and the complete experience of total freedom — always live in my heart. From this supreme reality come the three powers we all know: the power to wish (will), the power to know (knowledge) and the power to do (action). The whole universe is nothing but the shining play of its free power. And may this presence in my heart destroy everything that hides the secret wisdom of Lord Śiva's teachings. This one verse contains the entire book in seed form: oneness, freedom, the three powers, and the prayer to remove ignorance.

Here the author bows to his own master with deep love. In simple words: I am already free even while living in this body. How? By a few drops of compassion flowing like an ocean from my noble teacher Kalyāṇa, whose very name means good fortune. I take shelter in him, the true master, inside my heart. The commentary adds two precious points. First, the word 'means' (upāya) here does not mean outer rituals — it means the saving knowledge itself, the wisdom that carries you to freedom. Second, old books show this verse slightly differently, and the name Kalyāṇa is itself a blessing: the teacher is described as an ocean of good luck, and tradition remembers him as the master who taught Jayaratha, the commentator, merely by his loving glance.

The author speaks humbly about himself. In simple words: my heart has become hard and rough because of carrying the heavy load of worldly life for so long. Even so, I quickly place the Lord's teaching inside it — that teaching which sits like a shining crown jewel on the heads of all the kings of the earth. Meaning: this wisdom is the highest ornament; even kings bow to it. Though I feel unworthy and hard-hearted, I waste no time in sheltering this teaching within me.

Abhinavagupta tells us honestly why he is writing this huge book — and it is not for fame. In simple words: I am not writing to become famous as an author, nor to show off my beautiful language. My only wish is that my own thinking becomes pure and clean by staying busy day and night with this holy teaching. The commentary explains the key phrase 'purified thought': cleaning the mind of restless doubts and fixing it on the truth is itself a spiritual practice, belonging to the path called the Empowered Means. So writing this book is the author's own meditation.

The author looks around at people with sadness and wonder. In simple words: some ignorant souls keep coming and going — taking birth again and again without learning. Others burn with jealousy. Some are full of doubt. But what can we even say about those people who get the rare chance to hear this liberating teaching, yet do not even come to listen? The message is gentle but sharp: this wisdom is precious and rare; ignoring it when it comes to your door is the greatest loss.

Here is a warning about false teachers. In simple words: if a person has never truly heard this deep and sweet teaching, then whatever clever talk he gives to push people around — however skillful it sounds — comes only from his own selfish thinking and hidden motives, and it will only make listeners' minds shaky and confused. True teaching steadies the mind; clever talk destabilises it. So the seeker must check: does this teaching come from real wisdom, or only from someone's personal agenda?

The author closes his introduction with total humility. In simple words: my words are too weak for this great task. If you find anything hard to understand in this book, do not blame me for it — that difficulty is only the play of the Supreme Lord's own great bliss, which hides the truth and also reveals it, as He likes. The commentary adds the beautiful back-story: the teacher Kalyāṇa gave this wisdom to his student in one instant, simply through his loving glance — knowledge passed heart to heart, not through long speeches. And the word Trika itself is often lovingly called 'Half of Six', a secret name for this tradition. So the whole teaching is grace: hidden by the Lord, opened by the Lord, through the master's glance.

This is the famous first verse of the Tantrāloka, and it has two meanings at once — that is its beauty. In simple words: My mother Vimalā (whose name means Pure) found her greatest joy in giving birth to me; she lived in pure God-consciousness, and her energy is ever-fresh, always new. My father Narasimhagupta (his nickname means the hidden light with five faces) was a full, complete man with no empty desires, steady like the five-faced Lord. May my Heart — the divine juice (nectar) of the highest reality, born from the loving union of these two, Śiva and Śakti, father and mother — throb and shine everywhere! The commentaries open up every word: 'full-bodied' means containing everything like Lord Bhairava Himself; 'emission' (visarga) means consciousness endlessly pouring itself out and yet resting in itself — pure potential becoming everything; 'Heart' means the pulsing I-feeling where Śiva and Śakti are one; 'five faces' are the five powers — consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge and action — flowing into the world; 'ever-new' and 'hidden' are even hidden in the author's own name, Abhinava-gupta (ever-new + protected). Great masters read this verse in three ways at once: as praise of the supreme Goddess, as the union of Śiva and Śakti, and as the author's real human parents — all three true together.
